titulo: Moving Average Bounce Strategy: Trading the Pullback to the EMA 21
descricao: How the bounce off the 21-period exponential moving average works, with real Nvidia entries from 2026, position sizing, and common mistakes.
corpo:
Among trend-following strategies, the moving average bounce has a clear advantage: it uses a single indicator, it's easy to see on the chart, and it doesn't require memorizing a list of confirmations to start practicing.

The idea starts from a simple observation: in a trend, price rarely moves in a straight line. It advances, pulls back close to a moving average, and resumes direction. The strategy tries to enter on that pullback. In this guide we use real daily quotes for Nvidia (NVDA) between April and October 2026 to show an entry that worked, one that hit its stop, and a period when the rule said to stay out.

What the moving average bounce is

It's an entry in the direction of the trend, made at the moment price comes back to touch the moving average and shows it will keep going. In an uptrend, you buy when price pulls back to the average and closes back above it; in a downtrend, you sell on the mirrored move.

The most common choice is the 21-period exponential moving average (EMA), which reacts faster to recent price than a simple average of the same length. Shorter averages, like the 9, generate more signals and more false bounces; longer ones, like the 50, filter out noise but offer fewer opportunities.

How to calculate the EMA and the trade

The 21-period EMA gives weight k = 2 ÷ (21 + 1) = 0.0909 to today's close: today's EMA = close × 0.0909 + yesterday's EMA × 0.9091. With Nvidia, on September 24, 2026: close of $224.58 and previous EMA of $220.605 → 224.58 × 0.0909 + 220.605 × 0.9091 = $220.97, the same value platforms show.

The trade itself has three numbers, all defined before the entry:

  • Entry: the close of the candle that touched the average and closed back above it.
  • Stop: just below that candle's low.
  • Target: for example, twice the distance between entry and stop (a 1-to-2 ratio).

Real example: Nvidia and the EMA 21 in 2026

The chart shows Nvidia from April 1, 2026 ($175.75) to October 7, 2026 ($237.47), with the 21-period EMA. Three stretches show the strategy working, failing, and staying out.

September 24: the bounce that reached its target

The average had been rising again since September 17. On September 24 price pulled back to a low of $221.09, $0.12 from the EMA ($220.97), and closed at $224.58. Entry at $224.58, stop at $220.50, risk of $4.08 per share. 1-to-2 target: 224.58 + 8.16 = $232.74. On September 28 the high was $233.21 and the target was hit. On a $10,000 account risking 1% ($100), the position would be 100 ÷ 4.08 = 24 shares, for a gain of 24 × 8.16 = $195.84.

July 21: the bounce that hit the stop

The EMA was still rising, and on July 21 price touched the average (low of $204.01, with the EMA at $204.77) and closed at $207.29. Stop at $203.50, risk of $3.79. The next day the stock reached $214.39, but not the $214.87 target. On July 27 it fell to $195.44 and the stop was triggered. Two days later it closed at $190.01. A 1R loss, exactly as planned.

June: when the rule says to stay out

Between June 12 and June 24 the EMA sloped downward, from $211.16 to $208.37. Price did close above it on June 15 ($212.45) and on June 18 ($210.69), which looks like a bounce. But with the average falling, there's no uptrend to bounce in favor of. On June 24 the stock closed at $199.00, 6.3% below the June 15 close.

How to use the moving average bounce

Confirm the trend by the slope

Average rising and price above it most of the time: buys only. Average falling and price below it: sells only. Flat average: stay out, as in June.

Wait for the close

Touching the average isn't the signal. The signal is the candle closing back in the trend's favor after the touch. Price can simply cross the average and keep going.

Size the position from the stop

Position size comes from the accepted risk divided by the distance to the stop, as in the September 24 example. That avoids a lot that's too big for the stop or a stop too tight for the asset's normal noise.

Limitations

In very strong trends price almost never comes back to the average, and the strategy enters rarely: between April 8 and May 29 Nvidia closed above the EMA in 34 of 37 sessions. In sideways markets, price crosses the average several times and generates strings of small losses. And no single average period is the right one for every asset and timeframe.

Common mistakes with the moving average bounce

  • Buying on the touch, before the candle closes above the average.
  • Trading when the average is flat or sloped against the trade.
  • Moving the stop farther away when the bounce fails, as it would have been tempting to do on July 27.
  • Changing the average's period after every loss, chasing the perfect number.
  • Forgetting that the examples above describe what happened to Nvidia, not what will happen.

To practice without risking money, add the 21-period EMA to your asset's chart on a demo account and log every bounce: date, entry, stop, target, and result, including the ones you skipped because of the average's slope. After a few dozen cases, your own record shows whether the strategy works on the asset and timeframe you trade.
resposta: The moving average bounce is a trend strategy: in an uptrend, you buy when price pulls back to the average, usually the 21-period exponential moving average, and closes back above it. The stop sits below that candle's low, and the target is usually twice the risk. It only works with the average sloped in favor of the trade; in a sideways market, it generates losses in a row.
